{{Short description|Type of flame}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=December 2017}}
In [[combustion]], a '''Burke–Schumann flame''' is a type of [[diffusion flame]], established at the mouth of the two concentric ducts, by issuing fuel and oxidizer from the two region respectively. It is named after S.P. Burke and T.E.W. Schumann,<ref>Burke, S. P., and T. E. W. Schumann. "Diffusion flames." Industrial & Engineering Chemistry 20.10 (1928): 998–1004.</ref><ref>Zeldovich, I. A., Barenblatt, G. I., Librovich, V. B., & Makhviladze, G. M. (1985). Mathematical theory of combustion and explosions.</ref> who were able to predict the flame height and flame shape using their simple analysis of infinitely fast chemistry (which is now called as [[Burke–Schumann limit]]) in 1928 at the [[Proceedings of the Combustion Institute#History of Symposia on Combustion|First symposium on combustion]].

==Mathematical description==
Consider a cylindrical duct with axis along <math>z</math> direction with radius <math>a</math> through which fuel is fed from the bottom and the tube mouth is located at <math>z=0</math>. Oxidizer is fed along the same axis, but in the concentric tube of radius <math>b</math> outside the fuel tube. Let the [[Fuel mass fraction|mass fraction]] in the fuel tube be <math>Y_{Fo}</math> and the [[Mass fraction (chemistry)|mass fraction]] of the oxygen in the outside duct be <math>Y_{Oo}</math>. Fuel and oxygen mixing occurs in the region <math>z>0</math>. The following assumptions were made in the analysis:
* The average velocity is parallel to axis (<math>z</math> direction) of the ducts, <math>\mathbf{v}= v \mathbf{e}_z</math>
*The [[mass flux]] in the axial direction is constant, <math>\rho v=\mathrm{constant}</math>
*Axial diffusion is negligible compared to the transverse/radial diffusion
* The flame occurs infinitely fast ([[Burke–Schumann limit]]), therefore flame appears as a '''reaction sheet''' across which properties of flow changes
* Effects of gravity has been neglected

Consider a one-step irreversible [[Arrhenius law]], <math>\mathrm{Fuel}+s\mathrm{O}_2\rightarrow (1+s)\mathrm{Products}+q</math>, where <math>s</math> is the mass of oxygen required to burn unit mass of fuel and <math>q</math> is the amount of heat released per unit mass of fuel burned. If <math>\omega</math> is the mass of fuel burned per unit volume per unit time and introducing the non-dimensional fuel and mass fraction and the [[Stoichiometry]] parameter,

:<math>y_F = \frac{Y_F}{Y_{Fo}},\quad y_O = \frac{Y_O}{Y_{Oo}},\quad S = \frac{sY_{Fo}}{Y_{Oo}}</math>

the governing equations for fuel and oxidizer mass fraction reduce to
:<math>\begin{align}
\frac{\rho D_T}{r}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(r\frac{\partial y_F}{\partial r}\right) - \rho v\frac{\partial y_F}{\partial z} = \frac{\omega}{Y_{Fo}} \\
\frac{\rho D_T}{r}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(r\frac{\partial y_O}{\partial r}\right) - \rho v\frac{\partial y_O}{\partial z} = S\frac{\omega}{Y_{Fo}} \\
\end{align}</math>
where [[Lewis number]] of both species is assumed to be unity and <math>\rho D_T</math> is assumed to be constant, where <math>D_T</math> is the [[thermal diffusivity]]. The boundary conditions for the problem are

:<math>\begin{align}
\text{at}\, &z=0,\, 0<r<a,\, y_F=1,\, y_O=0,\\
\text{at}\, &z=0,\, a<r<b,\, y_F=0,\, y_O=1,\\
\text{at}\, &r=b,\, 0<z<\infty,\, \frac{\partial y_F}{\partial r}=0,\, \frac{\partial y_O}{\partial r}=0.
\end{align}</math>

The equation can be linearly combined to eliminate the non-linear reaction term <math>\omega/Y_{Fo}</math> and solve for the new variable

:<math>Z = \frac{Sy_F-y_O+1}{S+1}</math>,

where <math>Z</math> is known as the '''[[mixture fraction]]'''. The mixture fraction takes the value of unity in the fuel stream and zero in the oxidizer stream and it is a [[scalar field]] which is not affected by the reaction. The equation satisfied by <math>Z</math> is

:<math>\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(r\frac{\partial Z}{\partial r}\right) - \frac{\rho v}{\rho D_T}\frac{\partial Z}{\partial z}=0</math>

(If the Lewis numbers of fuel and oxidizer are not equal to unity, then the equation satisfied by <math>Z</math> is nonlinear as follows from [[Shvab–Zeldovich formulation#Shvab–Zeldovich–Liñán formulation|Shvab–Zeldovich–Liñán formulation]]). Introducing the following coordinate transformation

:<math>\xi = \frac{r}{b}, \quad \eta = \frac{\rho D_T}{\rho v} \frac{z}{b^2}, \quad c= \frac{a}{b}</math>

reduces the equation to

:<math>\frac{1}{\xi}\frac{\partial}{\partial \xi}\left(\xi\frac{\partial Z}{\partial \xi}\right) - \frac{\partial Z}{\partial \eta}=0.</math>

The corresponding boundary conditions become

:<math>\begin{align}
\text{at}\, &\eta=0,\, 0<\xi<c,\, Z=1,\\
\text{at}\, &\eta=0,\, c<\xi<1,\, Z=0,\\
\text{at}\, &\xi=1,\, 0<\eta<\infty,\, \frac{\partial Z}{\partial \xi}=0.
\end{align}</math>

The equation can be solved by separation of variables

:<math>Z(\xi,\eta) = c^2 + 2c \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{\lambda_n} \frac{J_1(c\lambda_n)}{J_0^2(\lambda_n)} J_0(\lambda_n \xi)e^{-\lambda_n^2\eta}</math>

where <math>J_0</math> and <math>J_1</math> are the [[Bessel function of the first kind]] and <math>\lambda_n</math> is the nth root of <math>J_1(\lambda)=0.</math> Solution can also be obtained for the planar ducts instead of the axisymmetric ducts discussed here.

<ref>Williams, F. A. (2018). Combustion theory. CRC Press.</ref><ref>Williams, F. A. (1965). Combustion Theory: the fundamental theory of chemical reacting flow systems. Addison-Wesley.</ref>

==Flame shape and height==
In the [[Burke-Schumann limit]], the flame is considered as a thin reaction sheet outside which both fuel and oxygen cannot exist together, i.e., <math>y_Fy_O=0</math>. The reaction sheet itself is located by the stoichiometric surface where <math>Sy_F=y_O</math>, in other words, where

:<math>Z=Z_s \equiv \frac{1}{S+1}</math>

where <math>Z_s</math> is the stoichiometric mixture fraction. The reaction sheet separates fuel and oxidizer region. The inner structure of the reaction sheet is described by [[Liñán's equation#Large Damköhler number|Liñán's equation]]. On the fuel side of the reaction sheet (<math>Z>Z_s</math>)

:<math>y_F = \frac{Z-Z_s}{1-Z_s},\, y_O=0</math> 

and on the oxidizer side (<math>Z<Z_s</math>)

:<math>y_F=0,\, y_O = 1-\frac{Z}{Z_s}.</math> 

For given values of <math>Z_s</math> (or, <math>S</math>) and <math>c</math>, the flame shape is given by the condition <math>Z(\xi,\eta)=Z_s</math>, i.e.,

:<math>Z_s=c^2 + 2c \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{\lambda_n} \frac{J_1(c\lambda_n)}{J_0^2(\lambda_n)} J_0(\lambda_n \xi)e^{-\lambda_n^2\eta}.</math>

When <math>Z_s\rightarrow 0</math> (<math>S\rightarrow \infty</math>), the flame extends from the mouth of the inner tube and attaches itself to the outer tube at a certain height ('''under-ventilated case''') and when <math>Z_s\rightarrow 1</math> (<math>S\rightarrow 0</math>), the flame starts from the mouth of the inner tube and joins at the axis at some height away from the mouth ('''over-ventilated case''').  In general, the flame height is obtained by solving for <math>\eta</math> in the above equation after setting <math>\xi=1</math> for the under-ventilated case and <math>\xi=0</math> for the over-ventilated case. 

Since flame heights are generally large for the exponential terms in the series to be negligible, as a first approximation flame height can be estimated by keeping only the first term of the series. This approximation predicts flame heights for both cases as follows

:<math>\begin{align}
\eta &= \frac{1}{\lambda_1^2}\ln \left[\frac{2c J_1(c\lambda_1)}{(Z_s-c^2)\lambda_1 J_0(\lambda_1)}\right],\quad \text{under-ventilated} \\
\eta &= \frac{1}{\lambda_1^2}\ln \left[\frac{2c J_1(c\lambda_1)}{(Z_s-c^2)\lambda_1 J_0^2(\lambda_1)}\right],\quad \text{over-ventilated},
\end{align}</math>

where <math>\lambda_1=3.8317.</math>
